name: DeepAgent

paper.title: DeepAgent: A General Reasoning Agent with Scalable Toolsets

construction.unit: folded memory: three JSON blocks (episodic, working, tool)
construction.kept_as: LLM summary of the agent's own reasoning and tool-call trace
construction.processing: auxiliary LLM compresses the full trace in three parallel prompted calls, one per memory type

organization.structure: three typed JSON blocks inserted into the task prompt
organization.stores: episodic memory (task summary, key events, progress); working memory (sub-goal, obstacles, next actions); tool memory (per-tool success rate, errors, derived rules)

management.operations: a fold drops the reasoning trace from the context and replaces any earlier folded memory with a new one
management.forgetting: raw trace leaves the context at each fold; at most 3 folds per task (code default)

retrieval.candidates: none: the whole folded memory sits in the prompt (tool search is dense retrieval over tool docs, not over memory)
retrieval.budget: 3 blocks; no length limit stated; at most 50 actions per task

use.context: original task prompt + 'Memory of previous folded thoughts' (episodic, working, tool) + question
use.reasoning: the main reasoning model restarts its reasoning from this prompt and keeps acting

classify.note: Memory is working context for one task: when to fold is a policy decision (trained with ToolPO), the content is written by a prompted auxiliary LLM, and the result is always read in full.

stages.ingestion: The agent's own interaction trace (thoughts, tool searches, tool calls and their results) grows inside one reasoning stream; long tool results (over 5,000 characters) are condensed by the auxiliary LLM before they enter it.
stages.construction: When the agent emits <fold_thought>, the auxiliary LLM reads the whole trace (and the tool-call history) and writes episodic, working and tool memory as three JSON objects in parallel.
stages.organization: Three typed blocks with fixed JSON schemas: episodic (task description, key events with step/outcome, progress), working (immediate goal, challenges, next actions), tool (per-tool success rate, effective parameters, errors, derived rules).
stages.update: Each fold rebuilds all three blocks from the full trace so far and replaces the previous memory in the prompt; the code allows 3 folds per task.
stages.retrieval: No memory retrieval: the folded memory is inserted in full before the question. Separate from memory, tools are found by dense search over tool documentation (bge-large-en-v1.5, top-10 in the code).
stages.answer: The main reasoning model (QwQ-32B) continues from the original instructions plus the folded memory and answers when done or at the action limit.
stages.learning: ToolPO (RL) trains the main model end-to-end with LLM-simulated APIs; the action-level reward includes a term for efficient folding, and its advantage is credited only to tool-call and fold tokens. The auxiliary memory writer is not trained.

summary: A reasoning model that finds and calls tools inside one thought stream and can choose to 'fold' its history: an auxiliary LLM compresses the trace into episodic, working and tool memory, and reasoning restarts from that memory.
notes: Venue: the paper's own ACM reference block and footers give WWW '26 (Dubai, April 13-17 2026), DOI 10.1145/3774904.3792460; arXiv comment 'Accepted by WWW 2026'. Text read from arXiv v3 (5 Feb 2026). Memory here is within-task context management, not memory across tasks or sessions: nothing persists between questions. The ToolPO training code is not in the repository, so the RL side (fold reward, tool simulator) is from the paper only.

sources.code_note: Commit 7febc95 (2025-10-26) is the first code release, days after arXiv v1; the folding, memory prompts and tool search are unchanged at the current HEAD (2e25aba, 2026-04-13), which only adds an Exa search option. The repository holds inference and evaluation code only; ToolPO training and the tool simulator loop are not released.

headline: The 'memory' is a compressed restart point inside one task: nothing is kept across questions.
Folding is the agent's choice (a special token); the summary itself is written by a separate, untrained auxiliary LLM.
Each fold summarises the whole trace from the start, including text already folded, and replaces the previous memory.

discussion.takeaway: Letting a reasoning model search for tools on demand and fold its own history into structured memory beats fixed ReAct-style workflows, most clearly when tools must be found in large open sets.

claims.claim: End-to-end reasoning with on-demand tool discovery beats workflow agents.
claims.evidence: Open-set ToolBench 64.0 and ToolHop 40.6 vs best baselines 54.0 and 29.0 (Table 1, §5.1).

claims.claim: Autonomous tool retrieval during reasoning is better than retrieving tools up front.
claims.evidence: Average 52.6 vs 28.5 for the best workflow method (Table 4, §5.5).

claims.claim: Memory folding matters for long-horizon tasks.
claims.evidence: Without folding the 4-task average drops 48.1 to 44.2 and GAIA 53.3 to 44.7 (Table 3, §5.4).

claims.claim: ToolPO improves over the untrained agent and over GRPO.
claims.evidence: GAIA 46.7 to 53.3, ALFWorld 88.1 to 91.8 (Table 2); higher, steadier reward curves than GRPO (Fig. 4).

discussion.limits_src: The paper has no limitations section.
reading: Memory here is per task and is rebuilt at each fold; nothing carries over between questions, so it is context compression rather than long-term memory.
The folding ablation is on the RL model and moves GAIA most (-8.6) while ToolBench moves 1 point; the paper does not report fold frequency or memory size, so how often folding fires is unknown.
In the code the tool list meant for the memory prompts is overwritten with an empty string, and every later fold re-summarises the full trace from the start.
The auxiliary LLM also condenses long tool outputs for all baselines (App. B), so the comparison with ReAct differs mainly in the reasoning model's control loop, folding and tool search.
Baseline numbers carry no statement of who ran them; OpenAI Deep Research and AgentLM rows have gaps that suggest reported numbers.

abstract.text: DeepAgent is a single-stream reasoning agent: a large reasoning model thinks, searches a tool index when it needs a tool, and calls tools without a fixed workflow. For long tasks it can fold its history: an auxiliary LLM compresses the trace into episodic, working and tool memory in JSON, and reasoning restarts from that. The model is trained with ToolPO, an RL method that uses LLM-simulated APIs and gives extra credit to the tokens of correct tool calls. Across ToolBench, API-Bank, RestBench, ToolHop, ALFWorld, WebShop, GAIA and HLE it outperforms workflow-based baselines, most in open-set tool retrieval.
